domains.title: Great Thing Lord of Mount Miwa
domains.subtitle: Mountain, Oracle, and Sacred Snake
domains.lead: Ōmononushi is the mysterious kami of Mount Miwa, one of the oldest and most enigmatic deities in Japan. He is associated with snakes, oracles, and the transfer of the land to Amaterasu's descendants. Unlike most kami, he had no image and was worshipped in the form of the mountain itself.

cards.name: Mountain God
cards.desc: He is identified with Mount Miwa itself, worshipped without an image.

cards.name: Snake Deity

cards.name: Oracle Kami
cards.desc: His will was sought through divination at Ōmiwa Shrine.

cards.name: Land Transfer
cards.desc: He is linked to the myth of ceding the land to the heavenly descendants.

mythology.lead: Ōmononushi's mythology is preserved in strange, archaic tales of snakes, possession, and oracles.

myths.title: The Serpent Husband
myths.text: A beautiful woman named Ikutamayori was visited at night by a mysterious lover. She became pregnant, and her parents asked her to identify him. She placed a needle threaded with red silk in his garment and followed the thread in the morning. It led to Mount Miwa and disappeared into a cave. The kami revealed himself as Ōmononushi, a great serpent, and asked to be worshipped. The child born from this union became an ancestor of the Miwa priestly line.

myths.title: Oracle of the Land
myths.text: When the heavenly descendants sought to take possession of the land, Ōmononushi — identified here with Ōkuninushi — was consulted. He declared that the land should be surrendered peacefully and withdrew to a hidden realm. His oracle made the transfer of sovereignty possible without war.

myths.title: Worship without Image
myths.text: Ōmiwa Shrine is one of Japan's oldest shrines and has no honden (main hall) housing an image. The mountain itself is the kami, and worship is directed toward its peak. This aniconic practice preserves an ancient stratum of Japanese religion.

lore.syncretism: Ōmononushi is deeply intertwined with Ōkuninushi and with the serpent imagery of archaic Shinto. He represents the mountain as divine body and the oracle as a means of negotiating sovereignty. His identification with Ōkuninushi shows how local kami were gathered into imperial mythology.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ōmiwa Shrine remains an active and revered site, attracting pilgrims who walk its cedar avenue toward the sacred mountain. The aniconic worship of Mount Miwa continues, preserving one of Japan's oldest forms of kami veneration.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ōmononushi is the god who has no face because the mountain is his face. He reminds us that the sacred can be a place rather than a person, and that some deities are worshipped best by looking up at a peak rather than into an image.
lore.archaeology: Ōmiwa Shrine at the foot of Mount Miwa is one of Japan's oldest shrine sites, with no main hall and worship directed toward the mountain. Archaeological work in the area has revealed ritual deposits and structures dating to the pre- and early historic periods.
